routes.name: Leave it with a partner
routes.fits: Before the company has the data to price the asset’s risk, or where a partner can own or finance the asset more cheaply
routes.condition: Enforce the risk transfer in contracts (insurance, guarantors, escrow, title); accept the partner’s share of margin and control; avoid dependence on one partner

routes.name: Own it and fund it with debt
routes.fits: Once repayment or utilisation data supports a lender’s credit decision and cash flows are predictable enough to service debt
routes.condition: Diversify lenders and repayment channels; match debt currency and tenor to the asset; size debt to downside cash flows and covenants (Moove shows the cost of a single repayment channel)

routes.name: Fund it from deposits under a banking licence
routes.fits: Where the company can obtain a deposit-taking licence and meet its capital requirements
routes.condition: Accept supervision and capital requirements; deposits fund lending only within prudential limits

routes.name: Own it and fund it with equity
routes.fits: For small or short-lived needs with no suitable lender, or where cash flows are too uncertain to service debt
routes.condition: Equity is usually the most expensive capital for an asset; keep the exposure small and time-limited

test.result: debt in substance, whatever the label

rows.text: Raise to validate, not to scale. Pivot before institutionalising (NALA).
Revenue, grants, prizes and accelerator money layered for minimal dilution (Autogirl, Feegor, Earthbond).
Partners carry vehicles, stock and credit.
Investors and sponsors who become partners (Wema Bank for Feegor). Identify the lead for the first priced round before grants run out.
Keep the cap table small enough to allow a pivot.
Delay institutional capital until the model is proven, and be able to show investors the delay is a choice.
Map every partner the model relies on for supply, credit or demand.
Keep costs and liabilities in the currency of revenue; avoid dollar liabilities against local-currency income.
State the likely exit early (Autogirl: trade sale).
Raise from strength, after proof of unit economics or profitability where possible. Do not size costs to an unraised round (Sendy).
Equity for the platform; receivables, asset-finance or working-capital facilities for the book or float once lenders will price it (NALA’s 2026 facility).
Bring assets onto the balance sheet, funded with debt, once data supports pricing and lenders are available (Omnibiz); otherwise stay with partners.
Lead investors based in the customer’s market (Highland Europe for LemFi); DFIs as lenders where their mandate is strongest (M-KOPA).
Protect ownership through instrument choice, not only through valuation.
Decline capital that funds expansion before one market is profitable.
Avoid repayments that depend on a single outside platform (Moove).
Borrow in the asset’s currency where local lenders exist; price hedging into any dollar facility.
Build an investor base whose return expectations fit that exit.
Raise counter-cyclically where the structure allows it (MNT-Halan, M-KOPA in 2023).
Debt at scale: securitisation, syndicated and sustainability-linked facilities. Equity for M&A and new markets.
Own the book where it is cheaper than partner funding; diversify funding sources, currencies and repayment channels.
Domestic institutions ahead of a local listing (MNT-Halan); strategic buyers ahead of a trade sale.
Measure dilution against assets financed, not equity raised.
Decline capital whose return expectations conflict with the likely exit.
Diversify lenders, partners and markets so no single exit or failure halts the business.
Use local debt markets and listings where available (MNT-Halan).
Plan the listing or secondary route; a domestic exchange works for local-asset businesses (MNT-Halan).
